title: High load impedance, headroom and gain

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
A resistor-loaded CS stage has gain \(2V_{RD}/V_{ov}\), so high gain means a large DC drop across the resistor. At a 0.2 V overdrive, a gain of 100 needs 10 V, which no low-voltage process has. The way out is a **current-source load**, usually a PMOS with its source at the supply and its gate at a fixed bias. To the signal it looks like its output resistance \(r_{op}\), tens of kilohms or more. At DC it needs only \(|V_{ov,p}|\) across it.

The gain becomes \(-g_m(r_{on}\parallel r_{op})\). Writing \(g_m = 2I_D/V_{ov}\) and \(r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D)\), the current cancels: the gain is set by \(V_{ov}\) and the two \(\lambda\)s, so lowering the current costs bandwidth, not gain. **Headroom** is the remaining constraint. The output can swing only between \(V_{ov,n}\) and \(V_{DD} - |V_{ov,p}|\). Because two high-impedance current sources meet at the output, small mismatches move the DC output a lot, and practical circuits fix it with feedback.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: At \(V_{ov} = 0.15\ \mathrm{V}\), \(\lambda_n = 0.06\) and \(\lambda_p = 0.09\ \mathrm{V^{-1}}\), the gain is \(-2/(0.15\cdot0.15) \approx -89\) at any current. On a 1.2 V supply with \(|V_{ov,p}| = 0.15\ \mathrm{V}\), the output can swing from 0.15 V to 1.05 V.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Assuming lower current lowers the gain at fixed overdrive.
- Forgetting \(r_{op}\) and quoting the intrinsic \(g_mr_o\).
- Expecting the DC output to sit at a predictable value without feedback.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Cascoding the load and the gain device multiplies both resistances, and the same load appears in mirror-loaded differential pairs.
